rv.q: The sheer verve and humanity of Rent shines through this revival.
This musical still burns brightly.

The Tom Stoppard Theatre (formerly the Duke of York’s) has been reconfigured to embrace a portion of the audience onstage, with the cast weaving through them and sometimes sitting among them before rising to sing.
This rousing, faithful revival by Paddington director Luke Sheppard more than earns its keep.
Rent manages that, and then some.
The revival is produced with devotion but, nudging three hours, also needs dramaturgical tough love.
Luke Sheppard’s 30th anniversary revival of this iconic musical reveals both its shortcomings and its enduring strengths
A formidable vehicle for Larson's songs, but a less impressive one for his story.
That sound you may be hearing most evenings toward the lower end of St Martin's Lane is likely to be the roof being blown off the Tom Stoppard Theatre...
This anniversary revival could just look back fondly – but, under Luke Sheppard’s electrifying direction, it instead packs an almighty punch.
This very fine, uplifting performance of one of the best shows of the year will raise your spirits and provide an insight into the way the world is organised.
This version of Rent deserves the hype it has been receiving and is a fitting tribute to the monumental legacy of a musician and creative genius that we lost far too young.
All in all, this is a hugely enjoyable revival of a musical that is standing the test of time, even as it conjures stories from the past.
This iconic musical captures the joy, uncertainty and resilience of a generation determined to make every moment count.
Rent is angry, sad, the band is rocking, the performers are crying, and the audience is too, as we can't help compare our own lives and hardships to those that have come before us.
Is it a terrific piece with notable performances from a talented cast? Undoubtedly.
The storyline seems tame rather than provocative these days, and the characters are noticeably well behaved.
It’s a flawless revival; one of the best shows I have seen all year.

Sheppard has created what we believe may well be the definitive production of RENT , a complete triumph from beginning to end, an extraordinary ensemble piece and a beautiful, bruising, joyful and heartbreaking tribute to Jonathan Larson.
This is the best version of RENT I’ve ever seen, proving what can be achieved when you put the right show in the right theatre at the right time...
If you like a good beat, good staging and very good acting, you'll feel this show in your bones.
Sheppard’s revival is a certain hit.
The show’s significance and relevance can be glimpsed in one of its very first lyrics: ‘How do you document real life / When real life’s getting more like fiction each day?’
It’s a grim, gritty portrait of the era set to a cracking rock soundtrack.
The definitive revival – every young LGBTQ person should see it.
With a little more emotional restraint and subtlety in the delivery of some of Larson’s songs, it could land with even greater force.

But by today’s standards, taking something so horrific as AIDS, which took the lives of 20,000 Brits alone, and putting it as a backdrop to a central story about people getting kicked out of their flats (which is dealt with with far more emotion) feels strange and tone deaf.
This is the definitive RENT revival.

RENT is the show to see in the West End, with a limited run, the generosity of the vocal talent and star-casting that truly works, it is a no-brainer for musical fans and newbies alike to get tickets.
This iteration – under the capable direction of Luke Sheppard and with a very talented cast of singers across the board – does not disappoint.
The evening's songs and multi-part harmonies are challenging, with the talent on stage representing musical theatre at its finest.
RENT will be safe as houses in London’s West End.
We would recommend seeking this out for a great production of a classic musical which has clearly influenced Lin Manuel-Miranda while reminding how Jonathan Larson could have been the next Sondheim.

Three decades on, this new version does not just pay homage to Larson's brilliant writing, but finds a new energy, underpinned by an exhilarating musicality that makes up for brief bloated moments, capturing the raw experiences of these characters with stark clarity.
Even without much in the way of freshness, and with moments of unevenness in the acting, this revival makes up for it with stunning vocal displays and a certain verve on stage.
If you’re coming for the songs and a talented cast, there’s plenty to enjoy.

But there's something scattered about this version, individual scenes and songs working well but the overall effect is disconnected making it far harder to follow for anyone coming to it for the first time.
But its poor execution makes this revival of Rent a weak tenant in the West End neighbourhood.

cn.t: Critics largely embrace this electrifying 30th anniversary revival, praising Luke Sheppard's propulsive direction and the ensemble's astonishing voices, though some find the production struggles to fully capture the show's deeper resonance.

vr.q: This Rent revival is the one that we have been waiting for.
